title: Turn PPR into Rental - when does CGT kick in?
body:
O.P.
Hi everyone:
If someone you know has lived in a place as their principle place of residence (PPR) for the last 10+ years, then they move out and turn it into a rental before later on selling the property, what happens with the capital gains?
1) Is the CGT exemption still applicable because they lived in it longer than they rented the place out?
2) Or are they taxed right away on the entirety of the capital gains once they turned it into a rental?
3) Or are they taxed on any capital gains from the assessed value of the property from the date they turn it into a rental? Eg, their property increased in value from $200k -> $500k while living in it. Now while worth $500k they rent it out and a year later it increases to $600k in value when they sold. 3a) Do they pay CGT on the entire increased value of $400k? 3b) Or only the $100k increase since turning it into a rental?
4) Or do they pay no CGT until they've rented it out longer than it was used as their PPR?
5) Or something else?
Thank you.

---- replies ----
[User #366088695 postsmexiwiWhirlpool Forums Addict] Depends on how klong they rented it out.
If it is less than 6 years they can still claim the exemption.
https://iorder.com.au/public ation/Download.aspx?ProdID=75488-04.2025
[User #190178195 postshmofWhirlpool Forums Addict] mexiwi writes...
If it is less than 6 years they can still claim the exemption.
That depends where they moved to.
[User #616533888 posts123enen2+2=4 0R 3+1=4 confused?Whirlpool Forums Addict] FireMyst writes...
3b) Or only the $100k increase since turning it into a rental?
Yes, that is the answer to your question. Only the increase since turning it into a rental is what you apply. Also, what Mexiwi said is correct. However, you can only claim CGT exemption on one property at the same one time- either this one (if less than 6 years) or any new one you may have moved into when this one was rented out.
[User #7769936075 postsTerry_wwww.structuring.com.auWhirlpool Forums Addict] Not enough info to answer for sure, but
If you mean 'main residence' then there is a possibility that the absent rule or the 6 year rule could be used to it could be fully exempt. But that depends on the circumstance and has consequences for any other property owned by you or your spouse (or dependent kid).
If it was first used to produce income when rented out then cost base would be reset to market value, generally, under s118-192 ITAA97 But this won't apply if it was previously rented.
[User #7769936075 postsTerry_wwww.structuring.com.auWhirlpool Forums Addict] hmof writes...
That depends where they moved to.
not really. They could move into a new main residence and still use the 6 year rule on the old main residence to keep it fully exempt (in some situations not all).
[User #893501059 postsengagedWhirlpool Enthusiast] FireMyst writes...
Eg, their property increased in value from $200k -> $500k while living in it. Now while worth $500k they rent it out and a year later it increases to $600k in value when they sold. 3a) Do they pay CGT on the entire increased value of $400k? 3b) Or only the $100k increase since turning it into a rental?
In your example "I think" you're also able to simply use the fraction of time owned as a PPR and Rental. In your example the total period owned is 11 years (10 PPR and 1 Rental) – Property has increased from $200K to $600K over this time. Therefore (1/11)*(600k-200k)=$36364 – and if owned as Rental >1yr eligible for 50% CGT discount – $18181....
[User #7769936075 postsTerry_wwww.structuring.com.auWhirlpool Forums Addict] engaged writes...
In your example "I think" you're also able to simply use the fraction of time owned as a PPR and Rental
No this wouldn't be possible because s118-192 requires the cost base to be reset if it was first used to produce income then.
But it could apply if the property was rented out just after settlement for example, s118-185 would apply then.
